Rollout: "GPT–6 Sol and GPT–6 Luna are rolling out in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today" for eligible paid users (Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, Edu), and both are in the API as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna. Free and Go users could try Luna only. Secondary sources (letsdatascience.com, dated Sept 22, 2026, and an OpenAI X post) say the same date and cite OpenAI's post "Introducing GPT-6 Sol and Luna" at https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-sol-and-luna/, but openai.com and X returned HTTP 403/402 to WebFetch, so OpenAI's own page was not read verbatim. Some sources give a Sept 17 launch date; that came from an unofficial account and is contradicted by the Sept 22 announcement. Later sources name a GPT-6.1 Sol (Sept 29 per ChatGPT release notes, as reported by a secondary source); that is a different model and is not used here. No separate preview before general availability was found.

GPT-6.1 Sol.quote: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29 at its annual DevDay developer conference.
GPT-6.1 Sol.kind_note: shipped model (API model ID gpt-6.1-sol; an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol, positioned below GPT-6 Astra)
GPT-6.1 Sol.note: Lab and kind notes confirmed. Availability at launch: API and ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid tiers, not standard ChatGPT chat (per Unite.ai and gradually.ai; a Korean report says not offered in the EU or UK at launch). Corroborating: gradually.ai lists 'Released' 'September 29, 2026' (label-value layout, not a sentence; https://www.gradually.ai/en/ai-models/gpt-6.1-sol/). 9to5Mac's DevDay coverage dated September 29, 2026 quotes OpenAI's announcement ('We're introducing GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that nearly matches GPT-6 Astra's intelligence on agentic coding, ...', https://9to5mac.com/?p=1071923). One Japanese outlet (gori.me) and ProPakistani (2026-09-30) are dated the 30th, likely due to time zones. Could not open openai.com (ProPakistani returned HTTP 403 and openai.com was not reached directly), so the date rests on secondary coverage quoting OpenAI's announcement; the primary OpenAI post was not opened. Not to be confused with GPT-6 Sol (released 2026-09-22 per one source) or the unreleased GPT-6.1 Astra, which OpenAI withdrew on 2026-09-28.

Gemini 2.0 Flash.quote: Gemini 2.0 Flash is now generally available, with higher rate limits, stronger performance, and simplified pricing.
Gemini 2.0 Flash.note: Lab (Google DeepMind) and kind (shipped model) confirmed. The first public availability was the experimental Gemini 2.0 Flash, announced Dec 11, 2024 and available 'to all developers' via the Gemini API, AI Studio and Vertex AI (quote: "Gemini 2.0 Flash is available now as an experimental model to developers via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio" and "with multimodal input and text output available to all developers"; https://blog.google/technology/google-deepmind/google-gemini-ai-update-december-2024/). Per the convention that a preview precedes general release, the GA date is recorded in release and the experimental date in preview_date. The Feb 5, 2025 Google post (https://blog.google/technology/google-deepmind/gemini-model-updates-february-2025/) says an updated 2.0 Flash reached all Gemini app users the week before; I did not open a primary source for that app rollout date, and secondary reports put it around Jan 30, 2025. Not settled: whether 'public' should mean the open Dec 11, 2024 experimental release instead. I followed the preview/GA rule, so Feb 5, 2025 is 'release' and Dec 11, 2024 is 'preview_date'.

MILO.kind_note: research prototype: an orchestration framework that discovers agent harnesses, described in an arXiv paper
MILO.note: Corrections: lab 'unknown' is still unresolved, since I did not open the paper's author affiliations. Kind 'harness' is off: MILO is a search and orchestration system that co-evolves agent harnesses and the strategy used to discover them, not a harness shipped to users. Source: 'MILO: Automated Harness Discovery via Orchestrated Multi-Agent Evolution' (arXiv 2609.38349; Hugging Face paper page https://huggingface.co/papers/2609.38349). I found no code repository, product, or launch announcement, and no public-availability statement. Reported results (Terminal-Bench 2.1, 86.1 ± 2.0%) come from the abstract and third-party summaries, not a released artifact. No date is sourced for the paper itself: the arXiv ID suggests a 2026 submission, and a lilys.ai digest URL is dated 2026-10-01, but neither is a release date. Unrelated 'MILO' products found and excluded: Miloverse's MILO (ALPHA) kids' creative AI app, FAAC's MILO VR training simulator, the miloteam Docker image, and the miloR R package.

Odin.kind_note: Unconfirmed: lab and kind notes given as unknown and harness; no single system identified
Odin.note: The name Odin matches several unrelated projects, and I could not tell which one, if any, is the target system. Candidates seen in search results: (1) Agnt/Odin, a minimalist CLI agent written in the Odin programming language (github.com/manelsen/agnt); (2) getodin.ai, a commercial no-code agent-building platform; (3) deepklarity/harness-kit, an open-source harness-engineering kit that includes a multi-agent orchestration CLI called odin; (4) OutlineDriven/odin-claude-plugin, a plugin for coding-agent harnesses, formerly the ODIN Claude Plugin; (5) Odin-Agent-, a personal agentic workspace. Uber's 'Odin' stateful platform is cluster infrastructure, not an AI system. Only search-result snippets were read; no candidate page was opened, and none gave a first public release date, so no date is recorded. The lab note 'unknown' and kind note 'harness' are not confirmed by any source. To settle this, the user needs to name the repository, company, or launch announcement for the intended Odin, after which its releases page or first commit can be checked.

PackingStar.kind_note: research prototype: a reinforcement learning system trained to find kissing-number configurations, not an agent harness
PackingStar.note: Kind and lab corrected. The kind 'harness' is wrong. The arXiv paper 'Finding Kissing Numbers with Game-theoretic Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 2511.13391) describes the system as 'a reinforcement learning system, PackingStar, to solve it', applied to the kissing number problem as a cooperative matrix-completion game. It is a research system, not shipped software. Lab: the 'Ma et al.' attribution fits first author Chengdong Ma; affiliations listed include Peking University's Institute for Artificial Intelligence, the Shanghai Academy of AI for Science, and Fudan University. The v1 submission date (17 Nov 2025) is a paper date, not a public-availability date, so it is not used as a release date. No sentence in the paper, and no GitHub repository, model release, or press report I found, says PackingStar was made publicly available for use. The 'agent harness' search returned an unrelated Peking University item, Harness-Zero, which I could not confirm has the same authors; it was not used. If a public code or model release is later found, revisit release_basis.

Qiushi Engine.note: Corrections to the input: lab was 'unknown'; it is Zhejiang University (College of Information Science and Electronic Engineering; lead researcher Yang Yihao, dean Chen Hongsheng). Kind was 'harness'; sources describe an autonomous research agent and do not use the word harness. The only dated event is the unveiling: China Daily (2026-07-21) says Zhejiang University 'unveiled an AI scientific discovery system on July 15' (2026). An unveiling is an announcement, not a release, so it is not recorded in 'release'. The same article says the system is expanding 'from internal research validation to broader real-world scientific applications' and is 'expected to' integrate more tools; it reports no public availability, waitlist, API, pricing or open-source license. The release_basis 'none_exists' rests on that internal-validation wording and on finding no public-launch report, which is a judgment, not a confirmed fact. Revisit if a public launch turns up. TTT-Discover.quote: Submitted on 22 Jan 2026 (this version), latest version 5 Feb 2026
TTT-Discover.kind_note: Test-time reinforcement learning method (training algorithm applied per problem) from the paper "Learning to Discover at Test Time"; not a shipped model or product.
TTT-Discover.note: Lab note is roughly right: first author Mert Yuksekgonul, with coauthors from Stanford, NVIDIA, UC San Diego, Together AI and others (last author Yu Sun). Kind note 'harness' is wrong: TTT-Discover updates the model's weights with RL during each problem, which makes it a training algorithm rather than an agent harness or orchestration system, so release_basis is none_exists. The quoted sentence is the arXiv posting date of the paper (v1, 22 Jan 2026), which I record for context only; it is not a product release date. Code is at https://github.com/test-time-training/discover (linked from the arXiv comments field). The paper is listed as an ICML 2026 spotlight; the arXiv page was opened directly, and third-party summaries (hyper.ai, VentureBeat) agree on January 2026. Results use the open gpt-oss-120b model via Tinker.

agent-afk.note: Lab noted as unknown; the repo belongs to an individual maintainer (named Griffin Long in a LinkedIn search result I did not open). The date is the project's own CHANGELOG.md entry for 0.1.0, which is headed 2026-02-09 and lists 'Initial release'. It conflicts with other sources: Stork (third-party directory, opened) says 'shipped Jul 1, 2026' and lists 'Founded: June 7, 2026', and a LinkedIn search snippet says development started in March 2026, which is later than the changelog date. I did not confirm when 0.1.0 became public: the npm page returned HTTP 403, and the npm registry JSON is about 7.9M characters, so I did not reach its 'time' field. The changelog entry does not say the release was public, so 2026-02-09 may be a private or pre-public build. Before treating it as public availability, check npm's first publish time for agent-afk@0.1.0. If that is in July 2026, the release date would be 2026-07-01 per Stork, though Stork is a weaker source.
